title: Laying on of hands
hook: believers pray with a hand on the shoulder of the one prayed for

segments.voice: Yesterday, praise: hands raised, songs repeated, David dancing in the street. Your line was hands up. When did your hands go up? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-one.

In Damascus, a disciple named Ananias hears the Lord tell him to go to a house on the street called Straight and ask for a man named Saul. Ananias knows that name. Saul has come to Damascus with authority to arrest people like him. He says so: he's heard how much evil this man has done. The answer comes back: go. So Ananias goes. He walks into the house where Saul sits blind, puts his hands on him, and says, "Brother Saul." Then something like scales falls from Saul's eyes, and he can see. Today's word is what Ananias did with his hands: laying on of hands.
screen: `A HOUSE ON THE STREET CALLED STRAIGHT.`

segments.voice: Through the New Testament, hands carry prayer. When parents bring children to Jesus, Mark says, "he took them up in his arms, put his hands upon them, and blessed them." Hands that bless. When the church in Antioch sends Barnabas and Saul out, "when they had fasted and prayed, and laid their hands on them, they sent them away." Hands that send. And on Malta, when the father of Publius lay sick of a fever, Acts says Paul "entered in, and prayed, and laid his hands on him, and healed him." Hands on the sick. James, too, tells the sick to call the elders of the church to pray over them. Pentecostal and charismatic Christians keep this close. When someone asks for prayer, others gather round, and a hand goes on a shoulder or a back while they pray, for healing, for strength, for the Holy Spirit. Other churches keep the gesture in their rites. Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and other churches ordain their ministers with the laying on of hands. In these passages, the hands come with words: a blessing, a prayer, a name. The prayer is to God; the hand says something to the person. Someone is standing with you, close enough to touch. Now go back to Ananias. The hands on Saul belonged to a man with every reason to be afraid of him. Before Saul could see anything, he felt those hands, and heard himself called brother. That's what makes this more than a gesture. It closes the distance between people before it asks God for anything.

Here's the practice, and it starts with asking. If someone you're close to is nearby, you can ask: may I pray for you, or may I hold you in mind for a moment? If they say yes, rest a hand lightly on their shoulder. If you're alone, bring someone to mind, and rest your own hand over your heart as you think of them. If you pray, you can pray for them in your own words, or simply say their name before God. If you don't, simply hold them with care. Keep it gentle and brief. The bell holds the time.
Laying on of hands. Praying with a hand resting on the person prayed for: to bless, to heal, to send, and to say someone is with you.
Your line: a hand and a prayer. Today, with permission, offer someone a hand on the shoulder and a word of care. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: In Pentecostal and charismatic churches, people who ask for prayer are often surrounded by others who pray with a hand on their shoulder; Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and other churches ordain ministers with the laying on of hands.

trapdoor: what you thought: a dramatic moment on a stage.
what it means: a quiet prayer with a hand on a shoulder, to bless, heal or send someone.
what a scholar hears: Hebrews 6:2 lists the laying on of hands among the first teachings of Christ; Acts uses it for sending and for healing the sick.

notes: Editor pass: removed the stock line 'you're not alone' (voice, word, screen); 'the hands always go with prayer' corrected, since Ananias speaks rather than prays (teach and myth); trapdoor no longer caricatures televised healing.
Ordination with laying on of hands attributed to 'Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and other churches'; confirm. Confirmation and chrismation left out to avoid misdescribing differing rites.
Pentecostal/charismatic prayer practice described generally; howItsDone says 'often'. Confirm.
Practice stresses asking permission before touch, per the outline; confirm wording is safe for all listeners.
Original: ἐπίθεσις τῶν χειρῶν (1 Timothy 4:14 has μετὰ ἐπιθέσεως τῶν χειρῶν); confirm form and pronunciation.
Acts 9:10–18 paraphrased apart from 'Brother Saul'; the street called Straight is from Acts 9:11.

Audit pass (serious): James 5:14 speaks of prayer and anointing, not hands, but was headed 'hands on the sick' and counted in the myth; replaced with Acts 28:8 (Paul lays hands on Publius's father) and James kept as a paraphrased aside. Acts 9:17 says 'putting his hands on him', not on his shoulder; 'the hand on Saul's shoulder' corrected.
